International Health Regulations Mar. 20, 2026 At a glance International Health Regulations (IHR) provide an overarching legal framework that defines countries mutual obligations in managing public health risks, events, and emergencies that have the potential to cross borders. CDC works with countries around the globe to comply with the IHR by building local capacity to prevent, detect, and respond to health emergencies. Overview The IHR 2005 represents an agreement between 196 countries that have committed to developing and maintaining specific public health capacities that enable them to prevent, detect and respond to public health threats within their borders. Furthermore, when an outbreak or other significant public health event occurs, these countries will report this event under the IHR for the awareness of all countries that are party to the agreement. These outbreaks, or significant events, are considered events of international public health importance. CDC works with countries around the globe to comply with the IHR 2005. Since an IoT product might be defined as including an IoT device and any other product components that are necessary to using the IoT device beyond basic operational features, there are risks that come along with this level of connectivity—especially among so many devices across the globe. pages.text: Invasive green crabs: If you can't beat them, eat them. | National Geographic By Kea Krause Photographs by Brian Skerry Published July 11, 2022 • 12 min read West Bath, Maine — If you close your eyes, a green crab scuttling up your forearm feels more spider than sea creature, its little legs picking their way as if spinning silk. If you open your eyes, you will see the forged work of 200 million years: bumpy carapace, plated apron, calcified pincers. The small crabs are exquisite, seemingly carved from jade. The big ones are monstrous looking. They are nimble and chaotic, and likely under any beach rock in the Gulf of Maine. But here, the European green crab is not native. It is an invader , a species that traveled to the region in the 1800s in the ballast water of trading ships. In the centuries since, the crabs have established a thriving population, feasting on soft-shell clams and blue mussels, overtaking fisheries that have sustained Mainers for centuries. Their monstrous appetites and canny ability to adapt and reproduce have outcompeted any efforts to remove them. Green crabs ( Carcinus maenas ) are an invasive species that first appeared in New England waters in the 1800s, mostly likely arriving in the onboard water of large oceangoing vessels. The species’ population has exploded in recent years due to warming seawater temperatures in the Gulf of Maine. Now, one of the last defenses against these marauding creatures is not to eradicate them, but to eat them . Apex predators, ichthyosaurs were the orcas of their time , stalking the seas more than 201 million years ago, during the Triassic period . Estimated to be more than 80 feet in length, paleontologists believe I chthyotitan could be the largest ichthyosaur ever discovered. Ichthyotitan’ s discovery dates to 2018, when University of Bristol paleontologist Dean Lomax and his team described a piece of ichthyosaur bone that had been found in the United Kingdom. On its back, an overlapping fan of stiff structures likely caught the light, vibrant with color. They looked very much like feathers, but were something entirely different as the reptile wasn’t related to birds or dinosaurs, and it existed a hundred million years before the first dinosaur took wing . Researchers have long believed things like feathers and fur—complex structures which grow out of the skin, and can be used for insulation, sensing surroundings, visual displays and allowing flight—are largely unique to the lineages that gave rise to birds and mammals. Historian Sam Dalrymple travels to Greece to meet an archaeologist who made the discovery of a lifetime. In 343 B.C., Philip of Macedon invited Aristotle, the greatest philosopher of his age, to join his court as tutor to his son as head of the Mieza Gymnasium. Aristotle would not have known it then, but his pupil Alexander the Great would go on to remake the world. Artwork by Armet Portanell, Look and Learn/Bridgeman Images By Sam Dalrymple Published October 30, 2026 I’m Sam Dalrymple , a historian and author of Travels of Samwise and Shattered Lands: Five Partitions and the Making of Modern Asia . Today we're diving into the discovery of Aristotle’s gymnasium. And we'll be back next week covering a controversial dinosaur fossil auction. Sign up here to make sure you don't miss it! I set out to meet archaeologist Angeliki Kottaridi in mid-August, as the temperature of the Pierian range had begun to drop, and the first of the wild cyclamen was beginning to blossom across the Greek countryside. Kottaridi is an energetic eccentric, who began her career studying witches in Greek myth and is now the proud owner of several dozen cats. A former assistant to archaeologist Manolis Andronikos, who found Philip of Macedon's tomb in 1977, Kottaridi later led the Greek excavation of Failaka, the most important Hellenistic site in Kuwait. Isaiah Rashad: Tiny Desk Concert August 25, 2026 5:00 AM ET Bobby Carter Credit: NPR Isaiah Rashad put everything into this Tiny Desk. And in the weeks leading up to the show, we came together to define what "everything" meant for this occasion. So much has happened since The Sun's Tirade in 2016, and through the music, Rashad wanted to talk about it all. As a result, the pride of Chattanooga crafts a performance that feels like a debut for longtime fans and newcomers alike. Only on NPR Isaiah Rashad: 'Time's up for being afraid of yourself' Rashad's music comprises just as much blues as hip-hop, and his strength lies in raw vulnerability, which he consistently expresses through honest songwriting. I spent two years mapping the areas surrounding one of the most beautiful drives in the world. Each morning, I looked forward to discovering and mapping an area adjacent to a one I did the day before. This diary entry serves as an introduction to a series of texts covering the challenges I encountered and how I overcame them. I have also added a “before and after” map excerpt, as well as a short video, to illustrate how my work gradually took shape over time. The Place The Icefields Parkway (Highway 93N), in Alberta, owes its name to the spectacular icefields and glaciers that line the road. pages.text: Join the search for the world's rarest wading bird in New Zealand | National Geographic TRAVEL Join the search for the world's rarest wading bird in New Zealand A new off-grid tour takes travellers deep into New Zealand’s largest basin in search of the elusive black stilt. New Zealand's Southern Alps are home to one of the world's rarest birds: the black stilt. Natasha Bazika By Natasha Bazika Published June 11, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Clouds move quickly across the Mackenzie Basin, dragging shadows over braided riverbeds and dry tussock plains that stretch towards New Zealand’s Southern Alps. One moment, the landscape is washed silver; the next, it disappears beneath a sweep of weather rolling over the mountains. I’m heading deeper into this high country on a window of borrowed time, crossing the 46,950-acre wilderness of Glenmore Station, a merino sheep, deer and cattle station. Hours earlier, the same storm front had grounded my helicopter flight to the country’s highest whisky bar — The Bad Decision, on a saddle above Glenmore Station — before it could leave the tarmac. Now, I’m racing a temporary clearing in the weather to find something far more elusive than a dram of mountain liquor: the black stilt, or kakī in Māori, one of the rarest birds on the planet. “The Mackenzie Basin has its own weather system,” says guide Ben Laffan, who’s taking me on Tekapo Adventures’ Black Stilt birding tour , a newly launched birdwatching experience, directing our four-wheel drive up a rough track. Juanes & Mon Laferte: Tiny Desk Concert May 23, 2018 5:00 AM ET Felix Contreras Credit: NPR Colombian pop star Juanes and Chilean singer Mon Laferte recently wrapped up a sold-out tour of the United States, which (lucky for us) included a stop at the Tiny Desk. Laferte began the concert solo with the torch song "Pa' Dónde Se Fue" (Where Did You Go?). She sang the break-up story with a smirk that belied the heartache hiding in her poignant lyrics. Then, after a short set break starring the Tiny Desk engineer Josh Rogosin, Juanes joined her to perform the duo's sultry single, "Amárrame" (Tie Me Up). It's rare to see Juanes in such an intimate setting. After almost two decades of performing solo, the Latin pop star is more of a stadium and arena kind of guy. It's a treat to hear his voice unencumbered by loud speakers or crowd noise, and to see his facial expressions as he sings lyrics that many of us know by heart. This marked a return to the intimacy that fueled his earliest days and that's still present in the personal lyrics that have sold millions of records. Sponsor Message That intimacy was heightened by the presence of Laferte. The duo performed a PG-13 version of "Amárrame," a passionate pop song with lyrics reminiscent of 50 Shades Of Grey . That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race. The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris. But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances. Jungle: Tiny Desk Concert November 2, 2026 5:00 AM ET Robin Hilton Credit: Photo: Lexy Beale/NPR It's hard for any band to make the old sound completely new, but Jungle has spent much of the past decade transforming vintage soul and R&B into something almost alien. The grooves are deep and warmly familiar, with wistful reflections on love and longing. But even in the brightest moments, there's often a thread of mystery and melancholy that leaves you questioning whether everything is as it seems. Fronted by the trio of Tom McFarland, Josh Lloyd-Watson and Lydia Kitto, Jungle is known for fluid live sets, with songs that spill into each other. True to form, at the Tiny Desk, they perform more than a half-dozen tracks that run together in a single, continuous groove. "We're gonna keep the music rolling," Lloyd-Watson tells the NPR crowd as the band melts seamlessly from 2018's "Beat 54 (All Good Now)" into "Dominoes" from the 2023 album Volcano. pages.text: Jurassic period information and facts | National Geographic SCIENCE What is the Jurassic period and why did it end? The heyday of dinosaurs, the Jurassic era saw Earth’s climate change from hot and dry to humid and subtropical. The Jurassic period was characterized by a warm, wet climate that gave rise to lush vegetation and abundant life. Many new dinosaurs emerged—in great numbers. Above, Dimorphodon reptiles fly over a herd of Mamenchisaurus dinosaurs coming down to a river for a drink. Illustration by CoreyFord, Getty Images By National Geographic Staff Last updated August 18, 2025 The Jurassic is a geologic period that took place about 201.3 million years to 145 million years ago and constitutes the middle part of the Mesozoic era . The Jurassic period was named after the Jura limestone deposits in the Jura Mountains, discovered by German geologist Alexander von Humboldt . Building on this find, French scientist Alexandre Brongniart later coined the Jurassic period. There are three Jurassic time periods: early, middle, and late. Overall, the Jurassic gives us a particularly well-preserved fossil record of prehistoric life, which included theropod dinosaurs that scientists believe evolved to become birds . Thanks to this rich record, we know that the Jurassic was the age of dinosaurs roaming a tropical Earth filled with ferns, flowering plants, and conifers. It was also a time when sea monsters, sharks, and blood-red plankton filled inland seas borne of crumbling landmasses. Here’s what the Jurassic period was really like. Justin Bis Justin Bis is the Chief of Staff for the Office of Technology Commercialization (OTC) at the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE). In this role, he works alongside OTC leadership to maximize the impact of DOE’s investments in technology commercialization, strengthen coordination across the agency, and ensure long-term success. He previously served at the White House as Special Assistant to President Trump and Deputy Director of the Presidential Personnel Office, where he managed the appointment of senior government officials responsible for regulating the U.S. financial and energy markets. At DOE, he was the Director of Intergovernmental and External Affairs under Secretary Dan Brouillette, serving as the department’s primary liaison to trade associations, labor unions, and state, local, and tribal governments. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn K2-Play Completes Final Phase of North Fruita Desert Trails Master Plan Oct 15, 2026 FRUITA, Colo. – Over the past eight years, the North Fruita Desert has changed in ways riders can see as soon as they arrive. There are more miles of singletrack, more places to camp and dedicated space for races and other large events, all part of a broader effort by the Bureau of Land Management and community partners to keep pace with one of western Colorado’s busiest recreation areas. This fall, the final trail in the North Fruita Desert Trails Master Plan is complete. K2-Play winds for about three miles along the base of the Book Cliffs and completes the final phase of a roughly 30-mile expansion of the 18 Road trail system. Its completion caps years of planning and construction involving the BLM Grand Junction Field Office, Colorado Plateau Mountain Bike Trail Association, Mesa County, City of Fruita, local businesses, professional trail builders and volunteers.
